messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 57

He arrived ten minutes early for every session, always sitting in the same chair near the door, never turning his back to the room. He is a man who has learned to read spaces the way he reads spreadsheets—for hidden inconsistencies, for the spaces where danger could hide.

Three years ago, he was not an accountant in a quiet Midwestern city. He was a junior auditor in his home country, a position that gave him access to records of government contracts. He made copies of documents he was not supposed to see. He thought he was careful. One evening, two men in civilian clothes met him outside his apartment building. They told him to come with them, and because he knew what happened to people who refused, he went.

The torture lasted six days. He does not describe the specifics easily—only that he was held in a windowless room with a concrete floor, that the electricity was intermittent, that he was made to listen to other prisoners being hurt. He was beaten, suspended from hooks, burned with cigarettes. He was shown photographs of his mother and told that if he did not cooperate, she would be brought in next. He gave them names. He gave them documents he had not actually seen. He signed a confession he could not read. Then, unexpectedly, he was released at night at the edge of the city with a warning.

Within a month, his uncle arranged papers. He fled to the United States as an asylum seeker. For the first year, he lived with a cousin and studied for his accounting exams, working double shifts at a warehouse. He passed. He got a job at a regional firm. He met a woman, married, moved to a suburb.

Now, at thirty-five, he is divorced. The marriage unravelled slowly. His wife would reach for him in bed and he would tense. She would ask him to go to the grocery store on a Saturday afternoon and he would invent reasons not to go—the crowds, the aisles with no clear exit. She wanted children. He could not imagine bringing a child into a world where men in civilian clothes could take anyone.

At work, he is meticulous, perhaps too meticulous. He checks and rechecks numbers, runs the same audit three times because his mind wanders. A door slamming in the hallway makes him lose his place. A colleague touching his shoulder from behind has left him shaking at his desk for ten minutes. His supervisor has noticed nothing—he completes his tasks, never late. But inside, the spreadsheet columns blur, and he sees instead the fluorescent light flicker in that concrete room. He will go to the bathroom and splash cold water on his face until the image passes.

He avoids news from his home country. He avoids movies with torture, but also movies with handcuffs, with basements, with loud arguments. He avoids walking home when it is dark and there are few people on the street. He avoids his mother's phone calls sometimes, because her voice carries an accent that reminds him of the men who interrogated him.

He is not angry. He is hollow. He will tell you, in his careful, measured accountant's voice, that he is fine. He will describe his symptoms as though they are audit findings—insomnia, hypervigilance, irritable mood—but the words come flat, detached. He does not say that he has not felt joy in two years. He does not mention that he stopped visiting his only close friend because the friend's laughter sounded like a threat.

Sitting across from him, you notice his hands rest on his thighs, perfectly still. He is watching the door. He is listening to the air conditioning unit kick on. He is calculating, always, the distance to the exit.
